thread.title: Youth & Family: Why awe matters - especially in winter
thread.title_full: Youth & Family: Why awe matters - especially in winter

author: Arwen Turner
title: Youth & Family: Why awe matters - especially in winter
text:
W inter can make the world feel smaller.
Days get shorter. People stay inside more. School feels heavier. Social life can get complicated. And for many young people, when winter sports aren’t accessible and money or transportation are barriers, winter can feel like an empty waiting room, a place where you’re left alone with your coldest, darkest and loneliest thoughts.
Add economic stress, and that weight grows heavier. Many families are feeling financial pressure from rising costs, unstable work and constant messaging around the holidays about buying more, doing more and having more. Research shows that when families experience economic stress, young people feel it, too. Youth are more likely to experience anxiety, depression, sleep issues and feelings of guilt or helplessness when money is tight at home. Even when no one says it out loud, young people notice.
Winter is also a powerful season for something we don’t talk about enough: awe.
Awe is that feeling you get when something makes you stop and think, whoa. It happens when you experience something big, surprising or meaningful, something that reminds you there’s more to the world than whatever stress is sitting in your brain at the moment.
Psychologists describe awe as a “self-transcendent emotion.” In simple terms, it pulls attention away from ourselves and helps us feel connected to something bigger than our day-to-day worries. Research shows that experiencing awe can reduce stress, improve mood, increase empathy and help people feel less anxious and isolated.
Outdoor athlete and writer Mirna Valerio talks about awe as more than a personal feeling. In her work, she describes awe as a collective experience, something that connects us to the land and to other beings, reminding us that we don’t exist in isolation. Awe helps us remember that we belong and that beauty is all around us.
Awe in the outdoors
A few days ago, I was having a rough day. I felt like I was disappointing everyone, and every decision I made seemed to upset someone. My thoughts were loud and anxious.
While driving between meetings, I noticed something out of the ordinary in a tree and pulled over. Above me sat a bald eagle, perched on a snowy branch, calmly watching the world go by. I stood beneath that tree for a few minutes, just taking it in, and felt my body soften. My thoughts shifted. Whatever had felt so heavy didn’t feel quite as overwhelming anymore.
Then the eagle spread its wings and took flight against a bright blue sky. I could see every feather. There was a loud whoosh … and then silence.
It was incredible. A moment of awe.
A lot of people think awe only happens in epic places like mountaintops or at expensive theme parks. But winter awe is often quieter and closer. It can be gazing at the moon on a cold night, the crunch of boots on fresh snow, a beautiful holiday light display or a friendly visit from a cardinal on a winter morning.
Awe doesn’t care how fast you move or how long you stay outside. Often, it shows up when you’re still long enough to notice.
Awe inside and together
Awe isn’t only found outdoors.
It can show up in music that gives you chills, a book where you finally feel understood, or the look in a child’s eyes when their elf on the shelf has done something magical they can’t explain. It can happen when you learn something new or notice how much you’ve grown, even if no one else has said it out loud.
Awe can also come from shared experiences. One of my favorite Christmas memories is from when I was 8 years old. My family was traveling to visit my grandparents when our car broke down in a small rural town, definitely not the Christmas we were expecting. Dinner came from a convenience store.
But when we got back to our room, my mom had turned it into a giant blanket fort filled with coloring books, pillows and blankets. We crawled inside and shared Nesquik straight from the container with a spoon. The disappointment of the day shifted into something warm and unexpected.
I look back on that moment now, and it’s still one of my favorite holiday memories.
Winter can be isolating, but shared experiences create connections and memories that last.
Why awe matters for kids
Young brains are still developing, especially the parts that manage stress, emotional regulation and perspective. Research from psychologists like Dr. Dacher Keltner at the University of California Berkeley, shows that awe can reduce rumination, increase empathy and help people feel more grounded and hopeful.
I was reminded of this recently when my teen dog walker stopped by with her 5-year-old sister. From inside the house, I could hear it had already been a hard day — big feelings in a small body. That morning, large icicles had formed along my porch roof. The younger sister suddenly stopped mid-complaint, climbed carefully onto the railing and broke off an icicle nearly half her height.
She held it like a magic sword. She was silent, wide-eyed and victorious. Her mood shifted. Not because someone told her to calm down, but because wonder stepped in and changed the moment.
Awe doesn’t fix everything. But it can soften things. It can help youth breathe a little deeper and make room for curiosity, hope and joy, even in difficult times.
Come experience awe with us
If you’re a teen looking for a moment of shared wonder, come experience awe with us at our immersive “Stranger Things” New Year’s Eve party from 7 p.m. to 12:15 a.m. Dec. 31. The event is free, but registration is required and space is limited for youth in grades 7-12.
This event exists because young people asked for it and because Sarah Graham, an occupational therapist in the Rutland Northeast Supervisory Union listened and reached out to us with a full event plan. The night will be “Stranger Things”-themed, with trusted adults, trivia, pizza, Eggo waffles, music, games and a live finale screening.
We’ll end the night sharing our hopes and dreams for the new year coming alive together, even when things can feel Upside Down.
More information is available at comealiveoutside.com/events.
Arwen Turner is executive director of Come Alive Outside.
